Not really a big deal. Regular troops have been out of Afghanistan for a long time. Operation Enduring Freedom ended in 2014, and was replaced by Operation Freedom Sentinel. This new operation saw the withdrawl of most conventional forces from Afghanistan, with only a couple brigades (5,000 - 7,000 strong combat unit) left doing TAA mission, which stands for Train, Advise, Assist. These new missions have them acting as instructors, supervisors, and backup for the Afghan forces, who took over the primary role of policing their own land and combatting the Taliban. U.S. conventional forces haven't been kicking down doors, leading foot patrols or manning checkpoints in any significant fashion for a long time.

Even more recently, the army replaced all the conventional forces in Afghanistan with these new all-volunteer SFAB units, which stands for Security Force Assistance Brigade. These new units fall under Special Operations Command, and are specially trained and deployed to conduct TAA missions. So now there's no conventinal forces left in Afghanistan at all. So these 7,000 troops returning are one of the SFABs redeploying (army lingo for coming back from overseas), and another one will probably deploy to replace them in a little bit. Or, more likely, the other 7,000 (which is another brigade) still in Afghanistan was their replacement, but their deployment wasn't publicised. Army practices RIP, or relief in place. When your units combat tour is done, you don't just pack up and leave, you wait for your replacement to show up, pass on knowledge, information and equipment they might need, and only leave once they're established and have taken over the mission. So two SFABs probably just finished RIP and the relieved unit is now coming back.
